utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are there any other matters before we turn to the Status Conference or, indeed, any matters for the Status Conference? Mr. Fila, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but there is a problem that we need to address. According to the Rules, it is very important whether the accused are cooperative, whether they assist the Court and so on. The accused Radic has spoken to Mr. Keegan and the police. I signed that tape as confidential. I was given one, the Prosecution, and a third for the Court. Without my knowledge and approval, those same tapes are in the possession of Mr. Krstan Simic. Personally, I don't mind, because I would have given them to him if he asked for them. But the question is, that I should like this Trial Chamber to address, if these tapes are given to anyone without the approval of Defence counsel, how sure can we be that people will be ready to cooperate, risking that what they are saying may be made public? Mr. Krstan Simic is a member of parliament of the Republika Srpska. He could have broadcast that at a parliamentary meeting. As we tend, in Serbia, to accuse each other of being traitors, that's the kind of people we are. This could happen too: Someone could say, "This one was a traitor." So I think a decision by the Trial Chamber would be desirable, a decision that would limit access to such material. In a way, we know that judgements are public and so on, but when something is of this nature, I fear that by such a ready access to such materials, the idea of cooperation with the Prosecution may be compromised. I apologise for raising this matter, but I feel that a ruling needs to be made. If you were to see that tape, you would see that it was stated there that without his approval, the tape would not be used, except for in the internal needs of the Prosecution, until it is tendered into evidence. It is a highly-delicate issue, and I would appeal to the Trial Chamber to make a ruling about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to that matter, firstly let me say that I am very concerned about anything that would interfere with potential cooperation between an accused person and the Prosecution, and I would like to assure counsel, all counsel for the Defence, that we are very sensitive to this. If we have created any concern by disclosing this material, then that's a matter that is of concern to us. The situation is, Your Honours, that counsel for other accused persons in this trial asked for the records of interview that have been conducted between other accused. In this case, we have one particular record, or I think there is more than one. There was a number of records of interview which we disclosed. We believed it was our obligation to disclose it under Rule 66, if the record of the interview was to be regarded as evidence against other accused persons. If it wasn't, if it was only to be evidence in relation to the accused who participated in the record of interview, then we wouldn't have believed that we had an obligation. So when we disclosed the document, we wrote a letter and said, "It is disclosed on the basis that the Prosecution will maintain that the evidence of that person is evidence against your client." Now, if there are any concerns about these records of interview being made prematurely public, because ultimately it's our intention to tender them in the course of the proceedings anyway as a public exhibit, but if there is concerns that they may be prematurely disclosed, we would remind Your Honours that the general order of non-disclosure should apply to Mr. Simic as well as anybody else. But if there is any concern about that, we join with and support the Defence in an order -- in seeking from Your Honours an order that if the Prosecution -- that in respect of any records of interview disclosed to other parties by the Prosecution pursuant to its obligation, that those records of interview not be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, just to assist, the tapes that we're talking about are interviews in relation to these events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it normally would be discloseable, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There's an argument, Your Honour, that if it's not to be used as evidence against the other accused, then our obligations under Rule 66, it's arguable we don't have an obligation to disclose it. The approach that I would like to take ordinarily is that they should be disclosed anyway because they are a matter that is going to arise during the trial. But I did take the precaution of having a letter accompany it, saying it was disclosed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Without prejudice, as it were, without finding what's happened in this particular case or, indeed, if anything has happened, would it be sensible then to make an order restricting the disclosure of the records of interview, as you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it would be sensible, because I am concerned about any issue that the Defence may raise which may interfere or hinder persistence with the Prosecution, so we would certainly ask Your Honours to do that. We can put it in a formal application, if Your Honours would prefer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll make the order. I think the legal officer will have sufficient for us to draw up an order. Yes. Are there any other matters, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session now for the final matters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session.
